Sergio,

Thanks for the quick intro earlier. Attached is NorthRidge's security questionnaire (NR_Sec_Q_Sept2027.pdf) — the vendor team needs targeted answers to the sections below for our procurement packet. Would you be able to deliver a short packet and an annotated network call flow by next Tuesday?

Emily — thanks for sending this over. We're preparing a concise packet that addresses each of the highlighted sections. Preliminary attachments for your review: segmentation-diagram-v2.png, isolation_matrix_v1.xlsx, threat-model-summary.pdf.

Quick notes up front:
- Control plane (management API, model registry, deployment orchestration) is on a separate VPC/subnet with strict egress rules and mutual TLS to worker nodes.
- Data plane (inference worker pools) is tenant-isolated by default — KV/prefix caches and model artifacts are per-tenant namespaces; shared caches are disabled for enterprise customers by policy.
- Egress is constrained via SNAT gateways and application-level allowlists; we also support customer-managed VPC peering where required.

Looping in Kimberly (Security) and Irene (Infra) to add technical details and the annotated call-flow you requested. We'll aim to have the final packet and a simple ASCII/annotated call-flow by Monday EOD PT. If NorthRidge prefers a short review call, we can arrange one next week.

Emily / team — adding technical detail for the packet; see inline answers below and the attached egress-control-playbook.md for operational controls.

On the topology:
- Control plane: isolated management VPC, private API endpoints, HSM-backed keys for signing model manifests. Access to control plane is limited to whitelisted operator IPs and customer-specific service accounts.
- Data plane: worker fleets run in clustered autoscaling groups. Each tenant gets a logically isolated namespace: filesystem mounts, Redis namespaces (if used), and model artifact directories are namespaced by tenant ID. We enforce RBAC at the orchestration layer so workloads cannot reference other tenants' artifacts.

Caching / KV behavior:
- Prefix/KV cache: tenant-scoped by default for enterprise deployments. Shared caching can be enabled only when explicitly requested and after a risk assessment.
- Model variants and fallback: variants live in the registry with access controls. Fallback to smaller/quantized variants is orchestrated by the routing policy and only routes to variants permitted for that tenant. No implicit cross-tenant serving of private artifacts.

Network controls and egress:
- Egress gating: workers route egress through SNAT gateways with per-tenant allowlists (application+destination). For private deployments we support forced tunneling to customer-managed inspection appliances.
- Sidecars: we run a lightweight sidecar proxy that handles TLS termination for model input/output, enforces per-request ACLs, and emits structured access logs to the control plane telemetry cluster.

Compromise/failure modes and mitigations (brief):
- Worker compromise (single host): we contain by eviction + KV namespace revocation; KV keys are short-lived and rotated on redeploy.
- Lateral movement: network ACLs + sidecar enforcements prevent east-west calls to management endpoints; only explicit service-to-service principals are allowed.
- Telemetry/audit: immutable logs to customer-controlled S3 (or vendor-managed with retention policy) and real-time alerts for anomalous token usage.

Evidence and artifacts attached: segmentation-diagram-v2.png (annotated), isolation_matrix_v1.xlsx (control/data plane mapping), egress-control-playbook.md (operational runbook). Also uploaded the packet to a shared drive: https://drive.redwood.ai/NR/packets/NR-2027-security-packet

If you'd like, Irene can share an example NAT/route table snippet and the exact audit retention configuration for enterprise customers.

-kim
Kimberly Park
Principal Security Engineer | Redwood Inference

Attachment: egress-control-playbook.md (Markdown, 14 pages)

Thanks — this all looks useful. A couple of follow-ups from our reviewers:

1) Can you confirm prefix/KV caches are tenant-scoped for the deployment model you described? Our threat model assumes a tenant cannot read another tenant's cached state.

2) We're particularly interested in the exact call-flow when a request enters the system (ingress -> sidecar -> worker -> model cache -> external logging). Can you provide a small annotated call flow (even ASCII) that shows the hops, protocols, and any trust checks?

3) For the control plane demarcation: do worker nodes ever initiate connections to the public control plane endpoints, or is it always the control plane that pulls from workers? We need to understand client-initiated vs server-initiated flows for our firewall rules.

If you can inline short answers for 1–3 and attach a tiny callflow, we can close the questionnaire.

Best,
Emily

Attachment: callflow-template.puml (for our diagram tool)

From: Sergio Alvarez <sergio.alvarez@redwood.ai>

Emily — answers inline and a minimal annotated callflow below. Attached also: callflow-annotated.txt.

1) KV/prefix caches: tenant-scoped by default in our enterprise offering. Cache keys include tenant id namespace and are backed by tenant-scoped Redis/managed in-process caches with encryption at rest. Shared caches are disabled unless explicitly requested and gated by an approval workflow.

2) Annotated call flow (minimal):
- Client -> NW LB (TLS, client cert optional) -> Ingress gateway (TLS offload, auth)
- Ingress -> Sidecar (mTLS) -> Request validation + per-request ACL (policy engine)
- Sidecar -> Worker runtime (local IPC / loopback) -> Runtime checks token and tenant id
- Worker -> Local cache (tenant-scoped) [cache hit: return; cache miss: fetch model artifact from model-store over secured channel]
- Worker -> Control plane telemetry endpoint (HTTPS) -> Append-only audit logs (customer bucket / customer-managed endpoint)
- If egress needed (external model fetch), request goes through SNAT gateway -> outbound proxy with allowlist

3) Control plane connectivity model: primarily control-plane-initiated orchestration (control plane polls worker status endpoints over a mutually authenticated channel). Workers establish an outbound TLS session to the control plane on startup for heartbeats (so most network setups only need to allow outbound to the control plane on port 443). The control plane does not open inbound connections to arbitrary worker hosts. For private deployments with strict firewalling, we support customer-managed peered control plane proxies so that all traffic remains inside the customer's network.

Next steps: we'll share the annotated PNG and the XLSX with field mappings to help your network team update firewall rules. If that works, let's schedule a 30-minute handoff with your infra/security folks—I'll send a calendar invite.

Regards,
